title: Dmp Hunt4c2
content:
DMP Hunt4C2 — .NET Memory Dump Analysis This walkthrough follows a .NET application from its call stack to its heap objects, then recovers an encrypted message from a Google Calendar event stored in memory.
The workflow:
Identify the .NET runtime → Find application objects and crypto fields → Recover the application assembly → Decompile the message-handling code → Read a Calendar event description from the heap → Decrypt the recovered messageThe addresses below come from this dump. For another dump, use the addresses returned by your own commands. Names such as CRYPTO_OBJECT_ADDRESS and BASE_ADDRESS are placeholders to replace before running a command.
1. Set up WinDbg and SOS Open the dump in WinDbg. Run these commands in the command box, one at a time:
.symfix .reload !eeversion !clrstack Command Purpose .symfix Configure the Microsoft symbol server. .reload Reload symbols using the configured symbol path. !eeversion Display runtime and SOS version information; a successful response also confirms that SOS is responding. !clrstack Display the current thread’s managed call stack. If WinDbg cannot find the SOS commands, try loading SOS beside CoreCLR:
.loadby sos coreclr !eeversion !clrstackThis loading method requires sos.dll to be available beside coreclr.dll. If it fails, load your installed SOS extension using its actual path:
.load C:\path\to\sos.dllThe stack contains coreclr and System.Private.CoreLib, which identify a modern .NET runtime. We use SOS to inspect managed memory and ILSpy or dnSpy to inspect the application code.
2. Find application objects Start with a summary of the managed heap:
!dumpheap -statLook for application-specific types among the framework types. In this dump, two useful leads are:
CSG2025_RC_Crypto CSG2025_RC_ComSearch for objects whose type names contain CSG:
!dumpheap -type CSGThe object rows include an Address column and an MT column. Use the object address with !do:
!do CRYPTO_OBJECT_ADDRESSUse the Address column here. MT is the MethodTable address, which identifies the object’s type; it is not the address of that object instance.
Read the crypto fields Inspecting the Crypto object revealed these fields:
key iv xorKeyFollow each field’s reference from the Value column. For a byte-array field, inspect its elements with:
!dumparray ARRAY_OBJECT_ADDRESSFor a string field, use:
!do STRING_OBJECT_ADDRESSThe heap contains the values present at the time of capture. We can recover those runtime values before understanding how the application originally encoded or decoded them.
For the final AES decryption in this walkthrough, the recovered values are:
key = b"rA8fT6YzX2pQ4eM9vW1kLdB3" iv = b"uJ7nP0xR3aH5bG2q"The supplied notes do not include an xorKey value. It is not needed by the final decryption script shown below.
3. Locate the application method Inspect the native stack and the managed stack:
k !clrstackThe relevant native stack excerpt is:
# Child-SP RetAddr Call Site 03 00000088`3979e8f0 00007ffd`a216580a ws2_32!recv+0xc1 04 00000088`3979e990 00007ffd`a21651f0 System_Net_Sockets!Interop.Winsock.recv+0xca 05 00000088`3979ea60 00007ffd`a2164def System_Net_Sockets!System.Net.Sockets.Socket.Receive+0x180 06 00000088`3979eae0 00007ffd`a2164b63 System_Net_Sockets!System.Net.Sockets.NetworkStream.Read+0x9f 07 00000088`3979eb60 00007ffe`01309864 System_Private_CoreLib!System.IO.StreamReader.ReadBuffer+0x63 08 00000088`3979ebb0 00007ffd`a2161d74 System_Private_CoreLib!System.IO.StreamReader.ReadLine+0x64 09 00000088`3979ec60 00007ffd`a2161949 CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge!CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge.CSG2025_RC_Srv.RemoteShell+0x404RemoteShell is calling ReadLine, which reaches the socket receive path. This suggests the thread was waiting for input when the dump was captured.
The RetAddr on the ReadLine row is 00007ffda2161d74. That is the return location in its caller, RemoteShell, so it gives us an address inside the application’s JIT-compiled method.
Resolve that code address with:
!ip2md 00007ffda2161d74Relevant output:
MethodDesc: 00007ffda2229398 Method Name: CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge.CSG2025_RC_Srv.RemoteShell(Int32) Class: 00007ffda2212528 MethodTable: 00007ffda22293d8 mdToken: 000000000600000C Module: 00007ffda21ee0a0 IsJitted: yes Current CodeAddr: 00007ffda2161970The field we need next is Module:
00007ffda21ee0a04. Export and decompile the assembly Inspect the module:
!dumpmodule 00007ffda21ee0a0Find its BaseAddress. Create C:\Analysis on your analysis machine if necessary, then replace BASE_ADDRESS below with the reported value:
!savemodule BASE_ADDRESS C:\Analysis\recovered.dllThe Module address from !ip2md identifies the runtime module structure. !savemodule needs the loaded image’s base address, which is reported by !dumpmodule.
Open recovered.dll in ILSpy or dnSpy, then trace:
Method or class What to inspect RemoteShell How commands are received and their results handled. CSG2025_RC_Crypto How crypto values are decoded and messages encrypted. CSG2025_RC_Com Where the message is stored and how it is sent. Microsoft documents the object, array, method, and module inspection commands in its SOS command reference.
5. Trace the Google Calendar message storage In the decompiler, open:
CSG2025_RC_Com → AppendTextToEvent()The method retrieves a Calendar event:
Event @event = service.Events.Get(text, eventId).Execute();The namespace import identifies the Event type:
using Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data;Its fully qualified name is:
Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data.EventThe method appends the message to the event’s description:
@event.Description = @event.Description + textToAppend + "\n";It then updates the Calendar event:
service.Events.Update(@event, text, eventId).Execute();@event is the local variable name. Event is its type. Searching the heap by the full type name lets us find event objects that may still contain the message.
These are decompiled code excerpts; we do not need to execute them or contact Google Calendar to read an event already present in the dump.
6. Recover the encrypted description Search for Calendar event objects:
!dumpheap -type Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data.EventFrom the results, identify the MethodTable for the exact Event type. In this dump it is 00007ffda2480c38.
List only the addresses of instances of that type:
!dumpheap -mt 00007ffda2480c38 -shortOutput:
0210af14b758 0210af1bcba0 0210af25d740Inspect the second event:
!do 0210af1bcba0Find the description’s backing field:
Value Name 00000210af1cc1b8 <Description>k__BackingFieldThe Value is a reference to a string object. Follow it:
!do 00000210af1cc1b8The recovered description contains this Base64 ciphertext:
xAYzbKdNTXbilYe1LgMrCwMvP0uu/6uhhT52MCnmzOTh2udnHKqJc/6iD+u9Bd3OIf one event has an empty or unrelated description, inspect the other event objects. A description can contain several appended lines; select the ciphertext line you intend to decrypt.
7. Decrypt the message The supplied script uses AES-CBC with a 24-byte key and a 16-byte IV. The key length makes this AES-192.
Install the dependency in your Python environment:
python -m pip install pycryptodomeSave this as decrypt.py:
import base64 from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Util.Padding import unpad ciphertext = ( "xAYzbKdNTXbilYe1LgMrCwMvP0uu/6uhhT52MCnmzOTh2udnHKqJc/6iD+u9Bd3O" ) key = b"rA8fT6YzX2pQ4eM9vW1kLdB3" iv = b"uJ7nP0xR3aH5bG2q" # Decode the ciphertext from Base64 into encrypted bytes. encrypted_bytes = base64.b64decode(ciphertext) # Decrypt with the recovered runtime key and IV. cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv) padded_plaintext = cipher.decrypt(encrypted_bytes) # Remove PKCS#7 padding and display the UTF-8 message. plaintext = unpad(padded_plaintext, AES.block_size) print(plaintext.decode("utf-8"))Run it:
python decrypt.pyVerified output for the supplied ciphertext, key, and IV:
!aB3@dE5#fG7^hI9&jK1*lM2(nO4)pQ6-rS8_tU0+vWThis verifies the decryption example. The dump extraction steps above are based on the recorded WinDbg output; the original dump was not re-examined while preparing this writeup.

title: Lro Rlo File Ext
content: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Build the RLO/LRO filename pattern shown in the M2 lab writeup.""" from __future__ import annotations import argparse import json from pathlib import Path RLO = "\u202e" LRO = "\u202d" def build_name(display_name: str, extension: str, prefix: str | None) -> tuple[str, str]: if not extension.startswith(".") or len(extension) < 2: raise ValueError("--extension must include its leading dot, for example .exe") if prefix is None: marker_at = display_name.lower().find(extension.lower()) if marker_at <= 0: raise ValueError( f"{display_name!r} has no {extension!r} inside it; supply --prefix " "whose text is the start of the display name and ends in the real extension" ) prefix = display_name[: marker_at + len(extension)] if not display_name.startswith(prefix): raise ValueError("--prefix must match the beginning of the displayed name") if not prefix.lower().endswith(extension.lower()): raise ValueError("--prefix must end with the real extension") remainder = display_name[len(prefix) :] if not remainder: raise ValueError("the prefix must leave some displayed text after it") # RLO reverses the remainder for display. LRO then starts a left-to-right # run containing the prefix. That prefix is last in the stored name, so its # final extension remains the file's actual extension. stored_name = RLO + remainder[::-1] + LRO + prefix return stored_name, prefix def main() -> int: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( description="Preview or apply the M2 lab RLO/LRO filename pattern." ) parser.add_argument("source", type=Path, help="Existing file, such as payload.exe") parser.add_argument("display_name", help="Name you want the UI to display") parser.add_argument( "--prefix", help="Displayed starting text ending with the source file's real extension; inferred when possible", ) parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="Rename the source file") parser.add_argument( "--literal", action="store_true", help="Print the raw Unicode name too; bidi controls are invisible", ) args = parser.parse_args() if not args.source.is_file(): parser.error(f"source file does not exist or is not a regular file: {args.source}") if "/" in args.display_name or "\\" in args.display_name: parser.error("display_name must be a filename, without directory separators") extension = args.source.suffix if not extension: parser.error("source file has no extension to preserve") try: stored_name, prefix = build_name(args.display_name, extension, args.prefix) except ValueError as exc: parser.error(str(exc)) remainder = args.display_name[len(prefix) :] destination = args.source.with_name(stored_name) print(f"Displayed name: {args.display_name}") print(f"Source file: {args.source}") print(f"Real extension: {extension}") print(f"Split: {prefix!r} + {remainder!r}") print(f"Escaped name: {json.dumps(stored_name, ensure_ascii=True)}") print("Controls: U+202E RLO, then U+202D LRO") if args.literal: print("Literal destination name follows; bidi controls are invisible:") print(stored_name) if args.apply: if destination.exists(): parser.error(f"destination already exists: {destination!s}") args.source.rename(destination) print(f"Renamed to: {destination}") else: print("Preview only. Add --apply to rename the source file.") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())python script.py file.exe 'CSG2025.Exercise.doc' --apply

title: Wireshark
content:
Use for: PCAP triage, conversations, file transfers, protocol inspection.
Run in: Windows GUI. Use TShark for CLI extraction.
First pass File → Open the capture. Check Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy, Endpoints, and Conversations. Apply a display filter in the top bar. Right click a relevant packet → Follow → TCP Stream or UDP Stream. Record the stream number and packet numbers. Display filters http http.request http.request.method == "POST" http.request.uri contains "flag" dns dns.qry.name contains "example" ip.addr == 192.0.2.10 tcp.port == 8080 tcp.stream eq 0 udp.stream eq 0 frame contains "flag" tls.handshake.extensions_server_nameframe contains searches packet bytes; reassembled content may require following the stream.
Walkthrough: recover an HTTP download Filter http and locate the request/response. File → Export Objects → HTTP. Select the object and save it into your output folder. Inspect it with the appropriate approved tool. For encrypted TLS, use Preferences → Protocols → TLS → (Pre)-Master-Secret log filename only when matching secrets are provided. A server private key alone does not generally decrypt modern TLS.
Gotchas Capture filter: host 192.0.2.10. Display filter: ip.addr == 192.0.2.10. No HTTP results? Check the port and Analyze → Decode As. Missing packets or a truncated capture can prevent reassembly. Reference: Wireshark User’s Guide.

title: OpenVPN Client
content:
Use for: connecting the competition PC to the challenge network.
Run in: Windows OpenVPN client. These steps describe OpenVPN Connect.
Connect Get the organizer’s .ovpn profile and any supplied credentials. Open OpenVPN Connect → import a profile from a file. Select the .ovpn, enter required credentials and connect. Confirm the client reports Connected. Open a supplied challenge endpoint in Chrome. Check Windows connectivity ipconfig route print # Replace with the assigned challenge host and port Test-NetConnection 192.0.2.10 -Port 443If Windows works but WSL does not # WSL: inspect addresses and route selection ip addr ip route ip route get 192.0.2.10Check the same endpoint from Windows and WSL. VPN routing and DNS can differ between them. Share that distinction with competition support if the provided setup fails.
Gotchas A failed ping does not prove the endpoint is down; ICMP may be blocked. Authentication failure, TLS/profile failure and a missing route are different problems. Keep the client connected while working on VPN endpoints. OpenVPN GUI and OpenVPN Connect have different menus; use the installed client’s import control. Reference: OpenVPN Connect profile import.

content:
Use for: browser challenges, DevTools, HTTP traffic, client side code.
Run in: Windows. No extra extension needed for these workflows.
Quick keys Action Key DevTools F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I Page source Ctrl+U Search loaded sources Ctrl+Shift+F inside DevTools Inspect element Ctrl+Shift+C Walkthrough: inspect a request Open DevTools → Network before performing the action. Enable Preserve log when navigation would clear requests. Reload or submit the form. Select the request; inspect Headers, Payload, Response, and Initiator. Filter Fetch/XHR for APIs or WS for WebSocket messages. Record the method, URL, cookies, body and response. Inspect browser state Use Application → Storage for cookies, local storage, session storage and IndexedDB.
// DevTools Console: inspect this origin's browser state document.cookie Object.entries(localStorage) Object.entries(sessionStorage) // Same-origin request using this browser session fetch('/api/status').then(r => r.text()).then(console.log)Gotchas HttpOnly cookies are absent from document.cookie; inspect them in Application. Client side validation can differ from server behavior; inspect the actual request. A Console fetch follows browser origin/CORS rules. Save useful responses and source snippets before changing state. Reference: Chrome DevTools Network guide.

title: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)
content:
Use for: running the tournament’s Linux CLI tools on Windows.
Run in: PowerShell to manage WSL; Bash inside the installed distribution.
Enter the supplied distribution wsl --status wsl --list --verbose wsl # Or choose a name shown above wsl -d UbuntuWindows ↔ Linux paths # WSL: replace Competitor with your Windows account cd /mnt/c/Users/Competitor/Downloads mkdir -p ~/ajcbbc/challenge01 cp challenge.bin ~/ajcbbc/challenge01/ cd ~/ajcbbc/challenge01 # Open the current WSL folder in Windows Explorer explorer.exe . # Convert path syntax wslpath -w "$PWD" wslpath -u 'C:\Users\Competitor\Downloads\challenge.bin'Windows Explorer can access Linux files using \\wsl$\<distribution>\home\<user>.
Basic workflow pwd ls -lah command -v python3 gdb binwalk exiftool sha256sum challenge.bin mkdir -p outGotchas Bash commands belong in WSL; PowerShell uses different quoting and syntax. Linux paths and filenames are case sensitive. Keep large processing jobs in the Linux filesystem for better performance. GUI tools need a functioning display/WSLg setup. SocketCAN and vcan depend on the supplied WSL kernel; installed can-utils alone is insufficient. VPN connectivity from Windows does not guarantee identical routing in WSL. Reference: Microsoft: working across filesystems.

title: Python 3
content:
Use for: byte manipulation, decoding, small solvers, artifact parsing.
Run in: WSL. Exact Python 3.x version depends on the competition PC.
Tournament rule: additional libraries are allowed except AI/ML related libraries and tools.
Quick commands python3 --version # Check the supplied interpreter python3 solve.py # Run a saved CTF solver python3 -m json.tool input.json # Pretty print an API response python3 -m zipfile -l archive.zip # List ZIP members before extraction python3 -m zipfile -e archive.zip out/ # Extract into a separate folder python3 -m venv .venv # Create an isolated package environment source .venv/bin/activate # Use that environment in this terminalWalkthrough: decode and inspect bytes Save as solve.py and run python3 solve.py:
from pathlib import Path import base64 import hashlib import re encoded = Path("input.txt").read_text().strip() data = base64.b64decode(encoded) Path("decoded.bin").write_bytes(data) print("length:", len(data)) print("sha256:", hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()) print(re.findall(rb"flag\{[^}\r\n]+\}", data))Byte recipes bytes.fromhex("666c6167") # Hex text → raw bytes int.from_bytes(b"\x34\x12", "little") # Decode a little-endian integer (0x1234).to_bytes(2, "little") # Encode an integer into two bytes # Repeating-key XOR: use the challenge's actual data and key data = b"example" key = b"key" result = bytes(b ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, b in enumerate(data)) # Modular inverse, when e and phi are coprime pow(65537, -1, 3120)Gotchas Use read_bytes() / write_bytes() for binary data. A Python str and bytes are different; specify encoding when converting. Do not use eval() to parse challenge input. Use json.loads() for JSON. Use uv for approved dependency environments. Reference: Python standard library.

title: uv
content:
Use for: Python virtual environments and approved dependencies.
Run in: WSL.
Tournament rule: do not install AI/ML related packages or tools. The same restriction applies to Python and other extensible tools.
Quick start uv --version uv venv --python python3 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip list python solve.pyWalkthrough: prepare a solver environment mkdir -p ~/ajcbbc/solver cd ~/ajcbbc/solver uv venv --python python3 source .venv/bin/activate # Non-AI libraries; install only what your solver needs uv pip install requests pycryptodome uv pip freeze > requirements.txt python solve.pyExisting requirements source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -r requirements.txt uv pip show pycryptodome deactivateInspect a supplied requirements file before installation to ensure it follows the tournament rule.
Gotchas Activate the environment in each new terminal or use its Python path explicitly. Crypto is the import namespace provided by pycryptodome. Package download access may be unavailable during the tournament. uv run can resolve dependencies; use the prepared environment’s Python when you want to run exactly what is already installed. Reference: uv environment guide.

title: gdb
content:
Use for: debugging Linux binaries, registers, memory and comparisons.
Run in: WSL. Use x64dbg for native Windows PE debugging.
Start gdb -q ./challenge # Open a binary with less startup text gdb -q --args ./challenge demo # Also supply its command-line argumentsUseful commands set pagination off set disassembly-flavor intel info files info functions break main run disassemble main info registers x/12i $pc x/32bx $rsp x/s $rdi si ni finish continue bt info breakpoints delete 1 quit Commands Purpose break main, run Stop when main starts info files, info functions Find entry points, sections and symbols disassemble main, x/12i $pc Read function/current instructions info registers, x/32bx $rsp Inspect CPU state and stack bytes x/s $rdi Read a string at the address in a register si, ni Step one instruction into / over calls finish, continue Run until return / next stop bt Show the call stack info breakpoints, delete 1 List / remove breakpoints Register examples above assume x86-64.
Walkthrough: inspect a comparison break strcmp run x/s $rdi x/s $rsi bt finish print $eaxThis example assumes a dynamically linked Linux x86-64 binary using the System V ABI: the first two pointer arguments are in rdi and rsi. For memcmp, also inspect the byte length in rdx; bytes may include NULs.
Gotchas A stripped binary may have no main symbol; use starti, info files, and instruction addresses. PIE addresses vary with the load address; derive runtime locations. Optimized/inlined comparisons may never call strcmp. run < input.txt supplies stdin from a file. Reference: GDB stepping and continuing.

title: objdump
content:
Use for: headers, sections, imports, symbols and disassembly.
Run in: WSL; supplied by GNU Binutils.
Quick commands objdump -f challenge objdump -h challenge objdump -t challenge objdump -T challenge objdump -p challenge objdump -d -M intel challenge > disassembly.txt objdump -s -j .rodata challenge Option Meaning -f File/architecture headers -h Section headers -t / -T Symbols / dynamic symbols -p Format specific headers, including PE import information -d Disassemble code sections -s -j NAME Dump a selected section Walkthrough: find validation logic objdump -d -M intel --disassemble=main challenge objdump -d -M intel challenge > disassembly.txt grep -n -E 'strcmp|memcmp|scanf|fgets' disassembly.txtRead the surrounding calls, branches and referenced constants. Move into Ghidra or gdb for data flow and runtime values.
Raw x86-64 bytes objdump -D -b binary -m i386:x86-64 -M intel code.binGotchas File offsets and virtual addresses are different. -D can decode data as instructions; plausible assembly is not proof of code. -M intel is relevant to x86 targets. Supported architectures/formats depend on the installed Binutils build; inspect objdump -i. Reference: GNU objdump manual.

title: strings
content:
Use for: quick readable text triage in binaries, images and memory dumps.
Run in: WSL; GNU Binutils.
Quick commands strings -a challenge.bin # Scan the whole artifact strings -a -n 6 challenge.bin # Suppress strings shorter than six strings -a -t x challenge.bin > strings_hex_offsets.txt # Retain byte offsets strings -a -e l challenge.bin > utf16le_strings.txt # Windows-style wide text strings -a -e b challenge.bin > utf16be_strings.txt # Big-endian wide text-a: whole file. -n: minimum length. -t x: hexadecimal offsets. -e l: 16-bit little endian, often useful for Windows text.
Walkthrough: hunt a clue strings -a -t x challenge.bin > strings.txt grep -niE 'flag|password|secret|https?://' strings.txt # Repeat for UTF-16LE strings -a -e l -t x challenge.bin > wide_strings.txt grep -niE 'flag|password|secret' wide_strings.txtUse the reported hex offset to inspect nearby bytes:
# Replace 0x120 with the offset you found xxd -s 0x120 -l 128 challenge.binGotchas No hit does not mean no flag; text may be encrypted, split or compressed. A hit may be a decoy or an unrelated string. Verify its context. grep -n reports the text output line number; strings -t x reports the binary offset. Huge dumps produce huge output files; start with targeted keywords and encoding choices. Reference: GNU strings manual.

title: zsteg
content:
Use for: bit plane and LSB steganography in PNG/BMP images.
Run in: WSL; Ruby gem already supplied.
Quick commands zsteg --help # Discover supported options zsteg image.png # Run normal image stego checks zsteg -a image.png > zsteg_results.txt # Search all supported combinationsWalkthrough: extract a detected channel Run zsteg image.png. Look for coherent text or a recognizable file signature. Copy the exact channel selector from that result. Extract it with -E and inspect the saved bytes. # Example selector; replace it with the result from YOUR image zsteg -E 'b1,rgb,lsb,xy' image.png > extracted.bin xxd -l 64 extracted.bin strings -a extracted.binRead the selector b1,rgb,lsb,xy │ │ │ └─ pixel traversal order │ │ └───── least significant bit interpretation │ └───────── selected color channels └──────────── one bit per selected channelGotchas -a is a broad search; false positives are common. JPEG is not this tool’s normal target format. Resizing or re-saving an image can destroy hidden bits; analyze the original. An extracted stream may need another decode/decompression step. Reference: zsteg usage and extraction examples.

title: binwalk
content:
Use for: embedded file signatures, firmware and appended data.
Run in: WSL. The approved list says latest; CLI details differ between v2 and v3.
Quick commands binwalk --help # Check this version's switches binwalk firmware.bin # Locate embedded file signatures binwalk -e firmware.bin # Extract recognized embedded content binwalk -Me firmware.bin # Recursively extract nested contentCheck the installed help for extraction options. The current upstream tool is a Rust rewrite; older online examples may target Python based v2.
Walkthrough: inspect an embedded file Scan the original file. Record the offset and identified signature. Try extraction and note the output directory printed by the tool. Inspect extracted files; a signature hit alone can be accidental. # Example: carve from decimal offset 4096 to EOF # Replace 4096 with a confirmed offset from the scan dd if=firmware.bin of=carved.bin bs=1 skip=4096 status=none xxd -l 64 carved.binIf the embedded object has a known length, add count=LENGTH to dd.
Gotchas Extraction may require external extractors that are absent on the PC. Recursive extraction can produce large output; start with a normal scan. High entropy suggests compression or encryption but does not distinguish them. Keep the source untouched and write recovered files separately. Reference: official Binwalk project.

title: ExifTool
content:
Use for: image/document metadata, GPS coordinates, comments and thumbnails.
Run in: WSL.
Quick commands exiftool image.jpg # Standard metadata overview exiftool -a -u -g1 image.jpg # Include duplicates, unknowns and groups exiftool -s -FileType -MIMEType image.jpg # Compare detected type with extension exiftool -GPSLatitude -GPSLongitude -n image.jpg # Numeric location clues exiftool -Comment -Artist -Author -Description image.jpg # Creator and hidden notes exiftool -json image.jpg > metadata.json # Save machine-readable metadata-a: duplicate tags. -u: unknown tags. -g1: group names. -n: numeric values without print conversion.
Walkthrough: investigate a photo Dump all metadata with -a -u -g1. Check location, creator, software, timestamps and comments. Compare metadata with visible clues. Extract a thumbnail if the tag exists. exiftool -b -ThumbnailImage image.jpg > thumbnail.jpg exiftool -b -PreviewImage image.jpg > preview.jpgAn absent thumbnail/preview tag can produce an empty output file.
Batch inspection exiftool -r -ext jpg -ext png -csv photos/ > photos_metadata.csvGotchas Metadata can be edited; treat it as a clue to corroborate. A leading minus option reads a tag; -TAG=value writes metadata. GPS reference tags matter when interpreting latitude/longitude manually. Check timezone information before correlating timestamps. Reference: ExifTool command documentation and official site.

title: pdftotext (Poppler utils)
content:
Use for: extracting searchable PDF text and preserving reading layout.
Run in: WSL; Poppler utilities.
Quick commands pdftotext -v # Check the installed Poppler version pdftotext document.pdf output.txt # Extract normal reading-order text pdftotext -layout document.pdf output_layout.txt # Preserve approximate columns pdftotext document.pdf - # Print text directly to the terminal pdftotext -f 2 -l 4 document.pdf pages_2_to_4.txt # Restrict extraction to pages 2–4 pdftotext -enc UTF-8 document.pdf output_utf8.txt # Request a specific output encoding- sends output to stdout. Page numbers start at 1.
Walkthrough: search a document pdftotext -layout challenge.pdf extracted.txt grep -niE 'flag|secret|password|https?://' extracted.txt # Compare reading order if columns or spacing are confusing pdftotext challenge.pdf extracted_default.txtRead the matching page in a PDF viewer to connect extracted text with the visual context.
Password supplied by challenge pdftotext -upw 'supplied-password' challenge.pdf output.txtGotchas A scanned page may have no text layer. pdftotext does not perform OCR. Custom font encodings can make extraction incomplete or scrambled. Hidden text may differ from what the viewer displays. Embedded attachments need qpdf or a viewer’s attachment panel. Reference: Poppler pdftotext manual source.

title: can-utils
content:
Use for: CAN bus capture, payload inspection and replay in automotive CTFs.
Run in: WSL with SocketCAN support. can0 is a real interface; vcan0 is a virtual interface.
Prepare a virtual practice bus # Requires kernel vcan support and permission to create interfaces sudo modprobe vcan sudo ip link add dev vcan0 type vcan sudo ip link set dev vcan0 up ip -details link show vcan0If modprobe or interface creation fails, the provided WSL kernel may lack support. Use the organizer’s supplied CAN setup.
Read frames # Terminal 1: watch timestamped frames candump -tz vcan0 # Save frames in canplayer-compatible log format candump -L vcan0 > capture.log # Show only standard CAN ID 0x123 candump 'vcan0,123:7FF'Send one known frame # Terminal 2: ID 0x123, four payload bytes cansend vcan0 123#11223344Classic CAN uses up to eight payload bytes. Decode the challenge protocol before assigning meaning to an ID or changing bytes.
Replay a captured log # For a log already recorded on vcan0 canplayer -I capture.log # Map a log's can0 frames onto local vcan0 canplayer -I capture.log vcan0=can0CTF workflow Capture a baseline → perform one action → compare IDs and changing payload bytes → replay the relevant frames → watch the challenge’s resulting state. A transmitted frame alone does not prove the objective completed.
Reference: Linux CAN utilities.

title: cannelloni
content:
Use for: tunneling CAN frames over an IP network into a local SocketCAN interface.
Run in: WSL with a working CAN/vcan interface. Use with can-utils.
Check the supplied build cannelloni -h ip -details link show vcan0Connect to a challenge CAN endpoint # Example values only: replace IP and both ports with organizer values cannelloni -I vcan0 -R 192.0.2.10 -r 20000 -l 20001 Option Purpose -I vcan0 Local CAN interface -R ADDRESS Remote IP address -r PORT Remote destination port -l PORT Local listening port -d cut CAN, UDP and timer debugging The remote endpoint must send back to your chosen local port. Match the supplied transport and addressing.
Observe the tunneled traffic # Second terminal; keep cannelloni running candump -tz vcan0 candump -L vcan0 > challenge_can.logTCP mode when explicitly supplied # Build must support this option; use the challenge's remote port cannelloni -I vcan0 -C c -R 192.0.2.10 -r 20000Gotchas UDP can lose or reorder frames. VPN routes, firewall rules and WSL networking can prevent return traffic. No frames? Check the CAN interface, protocol and ports before editing payloads. Cannelloni carries frames; it does not decode application command meanings. Reference: upstream usage and transports. The tournament list points to a fork; use the installed build’s help if options differ.

title: Zeek
content:
Use for: turning PCAP traffic into connection, DNS, HTTP and TLS logs.
Run in: WSL.
Generate logs from a capture # Logs are written into the current directory mkdir -p zeek_out cd zeek_out zeek -r ../traffic.pcap ls -lhIf checksum offloading prevents useful analysis, retry in a fresh output folder with zeek -C -r ../traffic.pcap. -C ignores checksum validation.
Pick the useful log File CTF use conn.log Who talked to whom, ports, timing and byte counts dns.log Queried domains and answers http.log Hosts, URIs, methods and status codes ssl.log TLS handshake metadata, when observed files.log Files observed by analyzers; not automatic file extraction weird.log Protocol anomalies Extract columns from default TSV logs zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h service < conn.log zeek-cut query answers < dns.log zeek-cut host uri < http.logGenerate JSON logs for jq # Run separately from the TSV example mkdir -p ../zeek_json cd ../zeek_json zeek -r ../traffic.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T jq -r '[.host, .uri] | @tsv' http.logGotchas Only observed protocols generate their associated logs. TLS application content remains encrypted without appropriate decryption elsewhere. Reuse the Zeek connection uid to correlate records across logs. Reference: Zeek quick start.

title: ZBar
content:
Use for: decoding QR codes and supported barcodes from images.
Run in: WSL; the image CLI is zbarimg.
Decode a QR image # Shows barcode type plus decoded value zbarimg code.png # Write only the decoded payload zbarimg --quiet --raw code.png > decoded.txtScan several images # Normal output retains image/scan context better than raw payload alone zbarimg *.png # Raw output for a known single image zbarimg --raw frame_001.pngCTF walkthrough Save the original QR/barcode image. Run zbarimg and keep the decoded value. Check whether it is a URL, Base64, hex, or plain text. Continue in CyberChef or Python if another encoding is present. If it does not decode Check whether the whole code and its surrounding quiet border are visible. Try a clearer supplied frame or image when available. A stylized, damaged or incomplete code may need reconstruction first. No result does not prove the image contains no hidden data; use zsteg/binwalk for other image clues. Check the installed build’s supported formats and options with zbarimg --help.
Reference: ZBar upstream project.

title: Burp Suite Community Edition
content:
Use for: intercepting HTTP, editing requests and comparing responses.
Run in: WSL GUI according to the supplied list; needs a working display.
Listed version: 2026.4.x; verify the competition build under Help/About.
Launch the supplied application # If the installation provides a launcher on PATH burpsuite # Alternative only when the organizer supplies a JAR and Java java -jar /path/to/burpsuite_community.jarWalkthrough: modify a request Start a temporary project with default settings. Proxy → Intercept → Open browser uses Burp’s configured browser. Browse to the assigned challenge. Find the request in Proxy → HTTP history. Right click → Send to Repeater. In Repeater, send the unchanged request to establish a baseline. Change one parameter; compare status, response length and body. Useful tools Tool Use Repeater Manually replay and edit requests Decoder Convert URL/Base64/hex representations Comparer Spot differences between responses Intruder Small controlled payload sets; Community has restrictions HTTP history Recover actual cookies, headers and request bodies Gotchas Leave Intercept off when ordinary browsing appears stuck. Repeater needs the correct target host, port and HTTPS setting. CSRF tokens and session cookies can expire. Windows Chrome talking to a WSL proxy may need additional routing/proxy setup; prefer the configured Burp browser when available. Community does not include the Professional automated scanner. Follow the tournament’s ban on AI related additions. Reference: PortSwigger getting started.

title: jq
content:
Use for: reading JSON API responses, filtering records and decoding log structure.
Run in: WSL.
Inspect structure jq . response.json # Pretty print jq 'keys' response.json # Top-level object keys jq 'type' response.json # Object, array, string, etc. jq '.items | length' response.json # Count recordsExtract fields jq -r '.flag' response.json # String without JSON quotes jq -r '.items[].name' response.json # Names inside an array jq '.items[] | select(.id == 7)' response.json jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .name] | @tsv' response.jsonCTF: search nested text values # Unknown schema: inspect all string values for a clue jq -r '.. | strings | select(test("flag|secret"; "i"))' response.json # Missing field fallback jq -r '.flag // .message // "no matching field"' response.jsonHandle JSON Lines and encoded JSON # One JSON object per line jq 'select(.status == 200)' events.jsonl # A field that itself contains JSON text jq '.payload | fromjson' response.json # Supply a string without shell interpolation inside the filter jq --arg name 'alice' '.items[] | select(.name == $name)' response.jsonGotchas Bash single quotes protect jq’s $variables from shell expansion. -r emits text and can lose JSON type/quoting information. jq parses JSON; HTML error responses will fail. Reference: jq manual.

title: Ghidra
content:
Use for: static disassembly, decompilation and validation logic.
Run in: WSL GUI per the supplied list. Listed version: 12.1.4.
Launch the supplied installation # Run from the installed Ghidra directory ./ghidraRunWalkthrough: find the input check File → New Project → Non-Shared Project. Import the binary, inspect the detected format/architecture, then open it. Accept auto analysis. Search → For Strings; search for success/failure text. Follow a string’s references to its caller. Read the Decompiler alongside the assembly listing. Identify input, transformations, constants and comparison length. Rename functions/variables and save the project. Useful navigation Action Common key/control Go to address G Rename selected symbol L References to selected item Right click → References Follow function Double click Inspect imports/functions Symbol Tree Show raw bytes Bytes field / Byte Viewer CTF notes Translate the validation loop into Python and reproduce it on known input. Check array sizes, signedness and endianness in assembly. An entry function is not always main; follow startup calls. Apply meaningful names as you learn what a value does. Gotchas Decompiled C is an approximation; verify surprising logic in assembly. A wrong architecture or image base gives misleading results. Packed/encrypted code may need runtime analysis in gdb/x64dbg. Reference: Ghidra beginner guide.

title: The Sleuth Kit
content:
Use for: disk partitions, filesystem records and deleted file recovery.
Run in: WSL. Autopsy provides a Windows GUI workflow.
Locate the filesystem # Find partition start sectors mmls disk.img # Example start sector: replace 2048 with YOUR partition's start fsstat -o 2048 disk.img-o is a sector offset, not a byte offset. For a filesystem-only image, omit -o. Confirm sector size from the image/tool output; -b can specify it when needed.
List current and deleted entries fls -r -p -o 2048 disk.img > file_listing.txt fls -r -d -p -o 2048 disk.img > deleted_listing.txt grep -niE 'flag|secret|password' file_listing.txtRecover a selected entry # Replace 12345 with the metadata address printed by fls istat -o 2048 disk.img 12345 icat -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered.bin # Attempt deleted-file recovery using its listed metadata address icat -r -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered_deleted.binOn NTFS, a listed address can include attribute components such as 12345-128-1; preserve the complete address.
Build a filesystem timeline fls -r -m / -o 2048 disk.img > bodyfile.txt mactime -b bodyfile.txt -d > timeline.csvGotchas Wrong partition offset produces misleading errors. Deleted content may be overwritten or incomplete. Extract evidence into a separate output directory. References: fls manual, icat manual.

title: OpenSSL
content:
Use for: Base64, hashes, certificate/key inspection and known-parameter decryption.
Run in: WSL; listed as OpenSSL 3.x.
Decode or hash a file openssl version openssl base64 -d -in encoded.txt -out decoded.bin openssl base64 -d -A -in single_line_base64.txt -out decoded.bin openssl dgst -sha256 challenge.bin-A is useful for Base64 supplied as one unwrapped line.
Inspect keys and certificates # Certificate subject, issuer and validity dates openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates # All certificate fields openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -text # Public/private key parameters openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -noout openssl pkey -in private.pem -text -noout # ASN.1 structure openssl asn1parse -in certificate.pemAdd -inform DER for binary DER input where the command supports it.
CTF: decrypt AES with raw key and IV # Example AES-128-CBC values; replace with challenge parameters openssl enc -d -aes-128-cbc -in ciphertext.bin -out plaintext.bin \ -K 00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff \ -iv 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f-K and -iv accept hex bytes. Password derived encryption uses different parameters:
# Prompts for a password; only correct if encryption used these parameters openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 10000 \ -in encrypted.bin -out plaintext.binGotchas Match mode, padding, salt, digest and KDF exactly. bad decrypt can indicate several parameter mismatches. enc does not support AEAD modes such as GCM. Reference: OpenSSL enc documentation.

title: xz
content:
Use for: decompressing XZ/LZMA streams and checking archive integrity.
Run in: WSL.
Inspect before decompressing xz --version xz -l evidence.xz # Size, ratio and stream summary xz -lv evidence.xz # More stream/block details xz -t evidence.xz # Integrity test; no extracted outputDecompress while preserving the input xz -dk evidence.xz # Explicit output filename; keeps original and writes bytes to stdout xz -dc evidence.xz > evidence.bin # Legacy .lzma stream xz --format=lzma -dc evidence.lzma > evidence.binCTF walkthrough Identify an XZ stream directly or through binwalk. Record its offset if it is embedded inside another file. Carve it, check integrity with xz -t, then decompress. Inspect the resulting bytes with xxd and strings. # Example embedded offset; replace 4096 with the actual value dd if=container.bin of=carved.xz bs=1 skip=4096 status=none xz -dc carved.xz > recovered.bin xxd -l 64 recovered.binGotchas xz -d normally removes the compressed input after success; add -k to keep it. .tar.xz decompresses into a tar archive, not its individual members. A raw LZMA stream needs the correct filter settings; it is different from a .lzma container. Reference: XZ manual.

title: qpdf
content:
Use for: PDF structure, decompressed objects, encryption and attachments.
Run in: WSL.
Check the document qpdf --check challenge.pdf qpdf --show-encryption challenge.pdf qpdf --show-npages challenge.pdf qpdf --show-pages challenge.pdfMake objects easier to read # Produces a separate PDF with readable object structure qpdf --qdf --object-streams=disable challenge.pdf readable.pdf strings -a readable.pdf | grep -iE 'flag|secret|JavaScript|EmbeddedFile'This is structural inspection, not guaranteed text extraction. Use pdftotext for normal page text.
Extract an attachment qpdf --list-attachments challenge.pdf # Use the exact key reported above; it may differ from the filename qpdf --show-attachment='attachment-key' challenge.pdf > attachment.binInspect and extract a stream object # Replace 12 with the relevant object number qpdf --show-object=12 challenge.pdf qpdf --show-object=12 --filtered-stream-data challenge.pdf > stream.bin--filtered-stream-data decodes supported stream filters; the result may still be binary.
Decrypt with a supplied password qpdf --password='supplied-password' --decrypt challenge.pdf decrypted.pdfGotchas Write to a new file to preserve the challenge artifact. Repairing/rebuilding can discard evidence from older PDF revisions. Object numbers and attachment keys are document specific. Reference: qpdf CLI manual.

title: llvm-mc (LLVM tools)
content:
Use for: assembling instructions and decoding short byte sequences across architectures.
Run in: WSL. Some distributions name the executable llvm-mc-VERSION.
Inspect the installed targets llvm-mc --version llvm-mc --helpx86-64: instruction → bytes printf 'mov eax, 42\nret\n' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --x86-asm-syntax=intel --show-encodingUse this to confirm a candidate instruction’s encoding while reading a CTF binary.
x86-64: bytes → instruction printf '0x90 0xc3\n' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --disassemble --output-asm-variant=1The example decodes a NOP followed by RET. The disassembler input is textual hex bytes.
AArch64 encoding printf 'mov x0, #42\nret\n' | llvm-mc \ --triple=aarch64-linux-gnu --show-encodingWrite an object file llvm-mc --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --filetype=obj input.s -o output.o objdump -d -M intel output.oGotchas An object file has headers and possibly relocations; it is not a raw byte blob. Match architecture, bitness, instruction mode and endianness. Some instructions need extra CPU features enabled. llvm-mc does not execute or emulate the instructions. Reference: LLVM llvm-mc manual.

title: xxd
content:
Use for: hex dumps, byte offsets, hex decoding and small binary edits.
Run in: WSL; supplied with Vim tooling.
Inspect a file header or region xxd -l 64 challenge.bin # First 64 bytes xxd -s 0x100 -l 64 challenge.bin # Region at hex offset 0x100 xxd -g 1 challenge.bin # One byte per group xxd -e -g 4 -l 64 challenge.bin # Display little-endian 32-bit groupsConvert bytes ↔ plain hex xxd -p challenge.bin > plain_hex.txt xxd -r -p plain_hex.txt > restored.bin # Decode a short known hex string printf '666c61677b64656d6f7d' | xxd -r -pMake a C-style byte array xxd -i challenge.bin > challenge_array.hCTF: patch a working copy cp challenge.bin patched.bin # Write one 0x90 byte at offset 0x20 in the copy printf '00000020: 90\n' | xxd -r - patched.bin # Confirm the modified region xxd -s 0x20 -l 16 patched.binGotchas Normal dump offsets are hex; do not confuse 0x20 with decimal 20. A patch uses a file offset, not a process virtual address. xxd -r can silently ignore text that is not valid dump data; confirm the resulting bytes. Use -r -p for plain hex and -r for an addressed xxd dump. Reference: xxd manual.

title: fsck.fat (dosfstools)
content:
Use for: diagnosing or repairing a FAT filesystem image.
Run in: WSL. Despite the tournament category, this is a filesystem tool.
Diagnose without changes # Use a FAT filesystem image, not an entire partitioned disk fsck.fat -n -v fat.img # Also list processed paths fsck.fat -n -l fat.img-n performs a noninteractive check without writing. Keep this option for initial triage.
Walkthrough: damaged FAT challenge Identify whether the artifact contains a partition table with mmls. If partitioned, extract the FAT partition first. Run the read-only check and save the diagnosis. Use Sleuth Kit to inspect recoverable entries. If repair is needed, do it on a copy and compare recovery results. # Example partition boundaries only: use values from YOUR image dd if=disk.img of=fat.img bs=512 skip=2048 count=65536 status=none fsck.fat -n -v fat.img > fat_check.txt 2>&1 # Repair the copy interactively cp fat.img fat_work.img fsck.fat -r fat_work.imgGotchas Repair can change directory entries, cluster chains and deleted evidence. Confirm sector size before using dd; 512 is only this example’s assumption. Do not run against a mounted filesystem or unrelated host drive. For file recovery, continue with The Sleuth Kit or Autopsy. Reference: dosfstools fsck.fat manual.

title: RsaCtfTool
content:
Use for: weak RSA keys, known RSA attack patterns and private key recovery.
Run in: WSL; Python based tool.
Check the entry point first # Current upstream CLI RsaCtfTool --help # Older supplied checkouts may instead use: # python3 /path/to/RsaCtfTool.py --helpUse the installed version’s help. Recent upstream uses --decryptfile; older examples often use --uncipherfile.
Inspect a public key RsaCtfTool --dumpkey --key public.pem openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -nooutTry a relevant attack # General weak-key recovery RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --private # Small private exponent candidate RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --attack wiener --private # Multiple supplied public keys RsaCtfTool --publickey '*.pub' --privateDecrypt challenge ciphertext RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --decryptfile ciphertext.binConfirm whether the challenge ciphertext is raw bytes, hex, Base64 or an integer before supplying it.
CTF notes Record n, e, ciphertext and any leaked factors/CRT values. Select an attack from the evidence rather than waiting indefinitely on all methods. Ordinary large RSA keys are not automatically breakable. Some attacks require optional dependencies or online services; availability and competition approval must be checked separately. Verify recovered plaintext bytes and padding; textbook RSA and OAEP differ. Reference: RsaCtfTool current CLI and examples.

title: Volatility 3
content:
Use for: processes, command lines, network state and files in memory dumps.
Run in: WSL. Examples use python3 vol.py from the installed checkout; a packaged installation may provide vol instead.
Discover plugins and identify Windows memory python3 vol.py -h python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.infoGlobal options such as -f, -o, -r, -p, and -s go before the plugin name. Use absolute artifact paths if running from the tool directory.
Windows CTF triage # Active processes and parent relationships python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pslist python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pstree # Scan for process objects and inspect command lines python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.psscan python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.cmdline # Network objects and file objects python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.netscan python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.filescanExtract files associated with a process mkdir -p /tmp/vol_out # Replace 1234 with the PID found during triage python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -o /tmp/vol_out \ windows.dumpfiles --pid 1234Export structured output python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -r json windows.pslist > processes.jsonLinux memory python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw banners python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslist python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pstreeLinux plugins require matching kernel symbols. Windows symbols can also need an available symbol cache or download access.
Gotchas Plugin names/options vary; inspect PLUGIN -h on the supplied build. Volatility 2 profiles and commands are different from Volatility 3. Empty results can reflect unsupported symbols or missing pages. References: Windows tutorial, Linux tutorial, dumpfiles plugin.

title: OpenSSH-Session-Key-Recovery
content:
Use for: recovering SSH cipher keys and IVs from a Linux memory image.
Run in: the supplied Volatility 3 installation in WSL. This entry is a plugin, not an independent CLI.
Required inputs Linux memory containing the relevant OpenSSH process/session state. Matching Linux kernel symbols for Volatility. Plugin openssh_sessionkeys.py and its openssh32/openssh64 symbol files. A matching PCAP if the challenge also requires traffic decryption. Discover the installed plugin # From the supplied Volatility directory python3 vol.py -h | grep -i ssh python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslistRecover keys from sshd # For a plugin integrated under the linux namespace python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw \ linux.openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys --name sshd --out /tmp/ssh_keys.jsonlUse the exact name listed in -h. An externally loaded plugin may appear as openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys instead.
External plugin/symbol directories # Discover names using the organizer's actual plugin and symbol paths python3 vol.py -p /path/to/plugins -s /path/to/symbols -h # Then use the reported name and the same -p/-s global options--pid 1234 can select a specific process instead of --name sshd. The upstream plugin writes one JSON object per line with --out.
Interpret the result Record the cipher name, key, IV, PID and session context. These are session encryption values, not the user’s login password. Recovering keys is only one stage; traffic decryption also needs correct direction, cipher/framing and capture context. Standard TLS key-log settings do not decrypt SSH.
Compatibility depends on the supplied plugin, Volatility API and OpenSSH structures.
References: project setup, plugin options and output.

title: x64dbg
content:
Use for: native Windows executable debugging, comparisons and runtime decoding.
Run in: Windows portable build. Use x64dbg for 64-bit, x32dbg for 32-bit targets.
Launch with a target # Run from the extracted debugger folder; adjust the actual location .\x64dbg.exe 'C:\CTF\challenge.exe'Useful controls Action Default key Open executable F3 Run / continue F9 Toggle breakpoint at selection F2 Step into F7 Step over F8 Execute until return Ctrl+F9 Restart Ctrl+F2 Walkthrough: find the check Open the executable and run to its relevant code. In the CPU disassembly, search the current module for string references. Find the failure/success message and follow its references. Set a breakpoint near the input comparison and run with a test value. Inspect registers, stack and pointed-to memory. Follow decoded strings or buffers in the dump view. Record the transformation and reproduce it in Python. Debugger command bar examples bp kernel32.GetProcAddress bp kernel32.LoadLibraryAThese help locate dynamically resolved APIs when the relevant exports are loaded and resolvable.
Gotchas Windows x64 integer/pointer arguments normally begin in RCX, RDX, R8 and R9. Linux gdb examples often use a different ABI. A patched success branch may skip flag generation; recover the actual input/algorithm. ASLR changes runtime addresses; keep module-relative offsets. Reference: x64dbg GUI manual.

title: Autopsy
content:
Use for: disk image browsing, deleted files, browser history and timelines.
Run in: Windows GUI. Uses The Sleuth Kit and additional ingest modules.
Walkthrough: investigate a disk image New Case → choose a case name and a separate output directory. Add Data Source → Disk Image or VM File → select the artifact. Set the source timezone from the challenge information. Select relevant ingest modules and start processing. Browse Data Sources, Views, and Results as results appear. Search the expected flag prefix and challenge keywords. Export useful files with Extract File(s) and record their source paths. Where to look Question Useful view/module What was deleted? Deleted file entries / filesystem views What did the user browse? Recent Activity / web artifacts Is a file extension misleading? File Type Identification / Extension Mismatch What happened at a given time? Timeline Is there hidden text or a named secret? Keyword Search Is an archive/document carrying another file? Embedded File Extraction Fast CTF workflow Start with likely user folders, downloads and deleted entries. Add focused searches while ingest runs. Correlate a hit with its full path, timestamps and neighboring artifacts.
Gotchas Some results appear only after the relevant ingest module completes. A keyword hit can come from metadata or an unrelated context. Preserve the original image and export recovered files separately. Use the tournament’s permitted modules; do not add AI/ML components. For CLI recovery see The Sleuth Kit.
Reference: Autopsy user documentation.

title: HxD
content:
Use for: raw byte inspection, file signatures, offsets and small patches.
Run in: Windows GUI; installer or portable build.
Walkthrough: inspect a suspicious file File → Open the artifact. Compare the first bytes with its claimed format. Search → Find → choose Text-string or Hex-values. Use Search → Goto to jump to a known offset. Inspect the data interpreter for selected integer/float values. Save edits as a separate working copy. File signatures to recognize Format Leading bytes PNG 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A JPEG FF D8 FF ZIP local header 50 4B 03 04 PDF 25 50 44 46 2D (%PDF-) ELF 7F 45 4C 46 Windows executable 4D 5A (MZ); verify the later PE header CTF: repair a known bad header Compare with the expected format → select the exact damaged bytes → overwrite in a copy → reopen with the relevant viewer/parser. A matching signature alone does not prove the rest of the file is valid.
Extract a byte range Use Edit → Select block to enter an offset and length, copy the selected bytes into a new file, then save with an appropriate name.
Gotchas Insert mode shifts later offsets; overwrite mode preserves file length. Distinguish hexadecimal and decimal offsets in dialogs. Endianness matters when interpreting multi-byte numbers. Changing PNG data can also require updating checksums. Reference: HxD features and usage.

title: TShark
content:
Use for: repeatable PCAP filtering, field extraction and stream recovery.
Run in: Windows PowerShell; included with the approved Wireshark installation.
Set the executable path $Tshark = 'C:\Program Files\Wireshark\tshark.exe' & $Tshark --versionIf already on PATH, replace & $Tshark with tshark. These commands also work with a supplied WSL binary after adapting shell syntax.
Triage protocols and conversations & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z io,phs & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ipExtract DNS and HTTP fields & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' ` -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'http.request' ` -T fields -e tcp.stream -e http.host -e http.request.uriRead a stream or save selected packets # Replace 0 with the relevant stream index & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -q -z 'follow,tcp,ascii,0' & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng -Y 'tcp.stream eq 0' -w .\stream0.pcapngExport HTTP objects New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\http_objects | Out-Null & $Tshark -r .\traffic.pcapng --export-objects 'http,http_objects'CTF gotchas -Y is a display filter; -f is a capture filter. -w saves packets, not decoded text. Live capture needs an appropriate interface/driver; offline -r does not. PowerShell continuation uses a backtick at line end, with no trailing space. Reference: TShark manual.

title: Notepad++
content:
Use for: source/log inspection, regular expression searches and small text edits.
Run in: Windows GUI.
Open an artifact from PowerShell # If installed in the default location & 'C:\Program Files\Notepad++\notepad++.exe' 'C:\CTF\output.txt'Useful keys Action Key Find Ctrl+F Replace Ctrl+H Find in files Ctrl+Shift+F Go to line Ctrl+G CTF: search a text dump Open the extracted text or source file. Ctrl+F → Search Mode → Regular expression. Search a pattern below. Choose Find All in Current Document for a list of matches. flag\{[^}\r\n]+\} https?://[^\s"'<>]+ (?i)(password|secret|token|api[_-]?key)Replace flag with the tournament’s actual prefix.
Search many files Ctrl+Shift+F → set the directory and a filename filter such as *.py *.js *.txt → enter a keyword → Find All. Open each hit with its file/line context.
Fix text representation Use View → Show Symbol for invisible whitespace, Edit → EOL Conversion for line endings, and the Encoding menu when the supplied text encoding is known.
Gotchas Choose Normal, Extended or Regular expression mode deliberately. Encoding conversion changes bytes; preserve the original artifact. Use HxD/xxd for binary edits. Notepad++ plugins may not be preinstalled; these steps use built-in features. Reference: Notepad++ search manual source.

title: dnSpyEx (dnSpy)
content:
Use for: decompiling/debugging managed .NET applications and assemblies.
Run in: Windows portable build. The supplied list specifies the self-contained win64 package.
Open an assembly # Run from the extracted dnSpy directory .\dnSpy.exe 'C:\CTF\challenge.exe'Walkthrough: recover a .NET check Open the EXE/DLL and expand the assembly tree. Find the entry point or UI event handler, such as a button click. Search strings for success/failure messages or the expected flag prefix. Follow the check into its methods and inspect constants/resources. Set a breakpoint before or after a transformation. Start debugging through Debug → Start with the proper runtime/arguments. Inspect locals, arguments and decoded arrays at the breakpoint. Reproduce the algorithm or save the relevant decoded bytes. Places to inspect Location Possible clue Main / startup code Argument checks, initialization UI event handlers Password/serial validation Static constructors Hidden constants, initialization routines Resources Embedded files and encrypted payloads Convert.FromBase64String callers Encoded values Crypto API callers Mode, key, IV and transformation Editing a working copy Use Edit Method or IL editing when available, then Save Module to a separate file. Record the original logic first.
Gotchas Native binaries need Ghidra/x64dbg instead. Obfuscation can make decompiled C# misleading; inspect IL and runtime values. A forced success branch can bypass the computation needed for the real flag. Target runtime requirements are separate from the debugger’s own self-contained package. Reference: dnSpyEx project and debugger features.

title: Eric Zimmerman's Tools
content:
Use for: Windows artifact parsing and forensic timelines.
Run in: Windows PowerShell, from the directory containing the supplied executables. Available tools/builds depend on the organizer’s installation.
Choose a parser Artifact Tool What it helps answer Prefetch .pf PECmd Program execution traces Event logs .evtx EvtxECmd Logons, process/service events NTFS $MFT / $J MFTECmd File records and filesystem changes Shortcut .lnk LECmd Target path and link metadata Jump Lists JLECmd Recently accessed application items Registry hives RECmd / Registry Explorer Configuration and user activity Generated CSV Timeline Explorer Sort/filter parsed results Parse execution and event artifacts # Replace C:\CTF\evidence with your extracted artifact folder .\PECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\Prefetch' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\prefetch' .\EvtxECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\evtx' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\events'Parse filesystem and recent-file traces # Single quotes preserve the literal $MFT name in PowerShell .\MFTECmd.exe -f 'C:\CTF\evidence\$MFT' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\mft' .\LECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\Recent' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\lnk' .\JLECmd.exe -d 'C:\CTF\evidence\AutomaticDestinations' --csv 'C:\CTF\out\jumplists'CTF walkthrough Identify the supplied artifact, then select its parser. Run TOOL.exe -h for the installed build’s options. Export CSV into a separate output folder. Open it in Timeline Explorer if supplied, or inspect it with PowerShell: Get-ChildItem 'C:\CTF\out' -Recurse -Filter *.csv Import-Csv 'C:\CTF\out\events\chosen-output.csv' | Select-Object -First 5Correlate timestamps, paths, users and IDs across artifacts. Prefetch presence supports execution analysis but does not alone establish who ran a program or its intent.
References: tool catalog, PECmd, EvtxECmd, MFTECmd, LECmd, JLECmd.
